title: The Good Thief
full_review:
An ex-con can't resist the lure of a huge heist and a foolproof alibi in writer-director Neil Jordan's densely plotted "The Good Thief" (Fox Searchlight).

A loose remake of 1955's "Bob le Flambeur," as a crime caper it's also dusted with the veneer of "Ocean's Eleven." While it's fine on seedy atmosphere and stunning Riviera visuals, eventually its ever murkier narrative turns wear the audience out -- and may leave them puzzled by the morally ambiguous conclusion.

Offering a captivating title performance, however, is Nick Nolte as washed-up, addicted ex-con Bob, living in Nice and first glimpsed shooting up in a disreputable nightclub.

When he saves cop Roger (Tcheky Karyo) from violent Algerian Said (Ouiassini Embarek), the cop merely turns the desperate immigrant into an informant on Bob, convinced his longtime nemesis is once again up to no good. Right he is.

Raoul (Gerard Darmon) and Paulo (Said Taghmaoui) present Bob with a heist plan involving the Monte Carlo casino that's too rich to refuse, only Bob goes it one better. His presence as a big-time gambler at the casino will be his airtight alibi since the cash-rich casino will only be a beard as the real heist is to take place a few miles away where priceless paintings are under supposedly impregnable electronic guard.

Realizing the cop and the informant are dogging his every move, Bob plans it so that attention will be on him as chief suspect and drawn away from the real scene of the crime.

Cuffing himself to his bed to go cold turkey off drugs, Bob's elaborate preparations require alarm systems expert Vlad (European director Emir Kusturica), brawny transsexual Philippa (Sarah Bridges) -- and the last-minute addition of conniving identical twins (director-brothers Mark and Mike Polish), who add a new level of risk to the proceedings.

Bob's a multilayered character; a repeat offender but with a genuine sense of honor and chivalry. He rescues a dissolute 17-year-old cocktail waitress (Nutsa Kukhianidze) from a likely descent into prostitution and refuses to take advantage of her sexual availability. He pointedly explains to the cop who the good thief hanging next to Jesus was, as if hoping he too will have a chance to truly repent before dying. But his weathered face shows he knows his crimes will come at a price he will have to pay -- if not in this world, then the next. Nolte makes his lived-in character fully credible and his buddy-enemy relationship with cop Karyo one of the pleasures of this film.

Jordan's technique is all over the lot -- at times sleek and engaging, yet just as often the shaky camera, fast cuts and mumbled dialogue are frustrating. The frequent cursing and glimpses of nudity add nothing, and the audience must pay close attention to keep up with the nuances of character and plotting.

Spiders figure in the execution of the heist, but by the end "The Good Thief" has become a rather tangled web.

Because of some violence, an implied affair and sexual references, fleeting nudity, brief drug abuse and much rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
